title: Kamala Harris says she has ‘not made a decision’ on potential 2028 presidential run – live
summary: Harris says she is ‘fully, sincerely focused on midterms’ as she speaks to conference in Nashville, Tennessee
body: In a court filing on Friday, the US attorney in Washington DC, Jeanine Pirro, moved to dismiss charges against David Hearn , a former Olympian her office had accused on vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. In asking to dismiss the criminal indictment, Pirro told the DC Superior Court that “it was not until after the return of the indictment,” that the Department of the Interior “provided additional documents” to prosecutors “indicating that damage to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in June 2026 was the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings (“AIC”), and the rush to complete the project prior to events associated with the America 250 celebration in the weeks surrounding Independence Day 2026.” “It was not until after these documents were produced,” Pirro added, that her office “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI.” “The Trump administration’s case against Davey Hearn should never have been brought,” Hearn’s lawyers, Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann and Steve Levin said in a statement. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim. The administration owes Mr. Hearn an apology.” In a social media post sent from Air Force One on Friday afternoon, Donald Trump drew attention to video of tens of thousands of migrants entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco the day before. “What’s happening with Spain,” Trump wrote, characterizing the arrival of migrants in the enclave on the North African coast that has been a Spanish possession since 1580 as an invasion, “happened in the United States during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration, and it will happen again, only worse, if the Dumocrats ever again gain power.” Trump illustrated his warning about the US-Mexico border with video of migrants crossing the border from Morocco into the Spanish territory that Morocco claims as its own, and calls “occupied”. This is not the first time that Trump has sought to sow fear about the US southern border by using video of migrants in Europe. In January 2016, Trump released an ad in support of his first presidential campaign that featured images of migrants surging across a border fence as a narrator promised that Trump would “stop illegal immigration by building a wall on our southern border that Mexico will pay for”. That video, however, was not recorded on the US-Mexico border, but in another Spanish enclave on the Moroccan coast, Melilla, in 2014. Trump’s closing ad for that campaign, released in November 2016 also featured footage of migrants in Europe, passed off as video of immigrants streaming across the border from Mexico into the United States. Near the start of that ad, as the candidate could be heard complaining of “massive illegal immigration,” thousands of people were shown walking along a highway. As I reported in 2016, however, that video was not shot along the southern border of the US — where Trump had promised to build a great wall — but in Hungary, at the height of the 2105 migrant crisis, and it showed Syrian refugees, desperate for safe passage to Germany, marching out of Budapest. That video was lifted, without permission, from a social media account of Nabih Bulos, a foreign correspondent who had accompanied the refugees. “When this footage was taken, thousands of refugees were on an odyssey through the Balkan corridor and Europe to escape the cataclysm ripping their country apart,” Bulos told me at the time. “As a son of two Palestinian refugees who benefited from Jordan’s largesse, a naturalized American welcomed to the country even after 9/11, as well as a working conflict journalist, the last thing I would want this footage to be used for is to embody Trump’s xenophobic, repugnant message.” Earlier this year, the Republican-led House appropriations committee referred to the dispute over the two enclaves in a report, in which it noted “that the Spanish-administered cities of Ceuta and Melilla are located in Moroccan territory and remain the subject of Morocco’s longstanding claim.” The committee added that it “supports efforts by the Secretary of State to encourage diplomatic engagement between Morocco and Spain on the future status of Ceuta and Melilla.” The US government released its anxiously awaited plan for how to manage the Colorado river crisis on Friday, outlining cuts in water supplied to California, Arizona and Nevada. The proposal from the US Bureau of Reclamation spares Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming from facing mandatory cuts, for now. But it is a temporary fix as the states that rely on the river continue to fight over a long-term management plan for the dwindling resource that supplies huge swaths of the western US. The proposal is the federal government’s answer to a years-long stalemate between the seven states responsible for forming a plan on how to distribute the deep cuts needed to pull the system back from the brink. It comes just months before the framework that currently governs the essential and imperiled waterway is set to expire. “This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the Basin States to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions,” said Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, in a press release. Under the 10-year plan, the Lower Basin states could face deep cuts of up to 3m acre-feet (3.7bn kiloliters) a year – up to 40% of their collective total – “subject to hydrology”, according to the press release by the Department of the Interior. That’s about enough water annually to serve more than 25 million people. The plan would also allow annual releases of between 5m and 12m acre-feet from Lake Powell, the basin’s second-largest reservoir. Under the 10-year federal framework, water management decisions will be made every two years. The federal government is expected to release a record of decision in the coming week that will detail operations under the plan in the short term, but it is likely they will closely follow a proposal issued by the lower basin states earlier this year that would shave 3.2m acre-feet from their combined total over 2027 and 2028. Senior Democrats accused Republicans in the US Congress of becoming “gelatinous blobs” who won’t stand up to Donald Trump and “rubber stamps” for his war on Iran. Elizabeth Warren, a US senator for Massachusetts, and Chris Van Hollen, a US senator for Maryland, argued that the Republican-controlled Congress had surrendered its constitutional authority to the president. In interviews with the Guardian, the senators urged their Republican colleagues to stand with Democrats and assert Congress’s authority as a separate branch of the federal government – with power over declaring war. “The Republicans have all had their spines surgically removed,” Warren said in Michigan, while stumping for the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. “I mean, they’re just gelatinous blobs that kind of make it through the United States Senate.” The constitution sets up three separate branches of government to hold one another accountable, Warren noted – and the assumption was that each of the three branches would “jealously guard its own powers”. Current and former prosecutors are denouncing the Trump administration for fast-tracking the deportation of immigrant children, as a key contract for legal services is set to expire on Friday. A series of federal laws has for decades shielded child immigrants from removal, either to protect their safety or to allow them to testify against abusers or human traffickers. But the Trump administration has undermined those laws, immigrant advocates and prosecutors say, by directing immigration judges to fast-track deportation cases for minors and blocking their access to lawyers who might help them apply for several forms of relief from removal – including acting as witnesses in cases of human trafficking or domestic violence. “By arresting and deporting survivors who have come forward and applied for protection, the Administration not only risks endangering the survivor and their family members, but the Government also sends a chilling message to the larger community: don’t call the police, don’t report crime – you or your loved ones will get deported,” reads a Wednesday letter to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from 10 current and former prosecutors. “This undermines public safety for us all.” Although Kamala Harris did not announce whether she would run for president in 2028, she did appear to signal a policy platform at the conference, saying: “We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts. We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and DC.” Kamala Harris also condemned Donald Trump’s decision to enter a war with Iran, saying: “I would have opposed it even if [Congress] had approved this war.” “They’re asking for hundreds of billions of dollars to pay for this war, meanwhile, you have people in America who are losing their health care every day, cannot afford their housing, cannot afford health care, cannot afford child care. There has been no articulation of the end game,” she said. Harris went on to say: “[Trump] is now talking about this deal. You know, the deal would basically be what Barack Obama got – that he pulled us out of,” referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action the US signed during the Obama administration which Trump pulled out of in 2018. “I think that it is important to not be a conspiracist, but at the same time, you can listen to what people are saying. And one, it just a full-on distraction from the things he can’t handle or has not handled. But this war is a war of choice that this president got into…

title: Labour wins decisive victory in Greater Manchester mayoral byelection
summary: Bev Craig, the city council leader, succeeds Andy Burnham as mayor, reversing Reform gains in May local elections
body: Labour has stormed to a decisive victory in the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection, seizing back areas that recently fell to Reform UK and the Greens. Labour’s Bev Craig, the Manchester city council leader, will now succeed Andy Burnham and hold one of the most powerful political positions outside Westminster. Labour won 47% of the vote, with Reform UK way behind on 21% and Greens in third on 12%. The contest took place under the supplementary voting system, meaning that as no candidate achieved more than 50% then voters’ second preferences were counted. When voters’ second choices were counted and other parties were discounted, Labour’s share rose to 66.3% and Reform UK’s to 33.7%. In her victory speech at the Co-op Live in Manchester, Craig urged society to “move away from divisive politics that try pit neighbour against neighbour”. The scale of the victory is a significant boost for the new prime minister, suggesting Labour can win back both left- and right-leaning voters who deserted the party under Keir Starmer. It also poses troubling questions for Nigel Farage, whose party has surrendered its year-long lead in the national polls and is in a deepening crisis over questions about its funding. A poll last month had Labour and Reform UK virtually neck and neck in the battle for the mayoralty. In the May elections, Farage’s party won more than 100 seats across Greater Manchester, including all but one of the 25 up for grabs in Wigan – the council of Burnham’s new constituency – and 18 out of 19 in Tameside, both once solidly Labour areas. However, Farage scuppered the party’s mayoral campaign when he announced he was standing down as an MP in order to fight a self-imposed parliamentary byelection in Clacton after scrutiny over his funding. Before the result was officially declared, Labour sources said it had won in every ward in boroughs including Bury, Tameside and all but one Trafford, where both Reform UK and the Greens made inroads in May. In Oldham, where Reform UK gained 13 councillors and ended Labour’s 15-year grip in power two months ago, Labour won 17 of the 20 wards in the mayoral contest, it is understood. Sources said Labour had won every ward in Gorton and Denton, the constituency won by the Green party’s Hannah Spencer in February. One senior Labour source said it looked as if Reform UK had “massively underperformed” and that the result was a combination of Burnham’s prime ministership signalling “you can vote Labour again” and voters feeling confident they could vote for Craig. Speaking from the podium after the result was announced just after 11pm on Friday, Craig said that during the campaign she had met “fantastic people doing incredible things against the odds every single day – rejecting the politics of hate but standing with their neighbours, looking out for each other”. For the Greens, which won 7% of the vote against Burnham when the Greater Manchester mayoralty was last contested in 2024, the result may be a disappointment after its recent electoral successes. Geraldine Coggins, the Green party candidate, said she was pleased with its campaign and that there had been a “surge” of support for the party under Zack Polanski’s leadership. She claimed the result was “not a ringing endorsement” of Craig, comparing her 47% vote share with Burnham who never won less than 60% of the vote in each of his three victories since 2017. “The fact this has even gone to the second round is devastating for them,” Coggins said. “To have lost this much support in the honeymoon period of a new prime minister is not a positive sign for them.” The contest was triggered by Burnham winning the Makerfield byelection on 18 June, meaning he had to step down as mayor of the most powerful combined authority outside London. The byelection was the biggest contest of its kind in British political history, with more than 2 million eligible voters. However, the turnout was down on previous Greater Manchester mayoral contests – only 25%, the third lowest of any mayoral byelection to date – due to a combination of low voter awareness and it taking place in the summer holidays.

title: Missing Australian hiker found dead in Wyoming, officials say
summary: Body of William Standish discovered in Teton mountains as investigators say fatal fall likely cause of death
body: A 28-year-old Australian hiker who lost contact with his family while hiking the Continental Divide Trail between Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks in Wyoming has been found dead, according to authorities. The man, identified as William Standish, was discovered by rescuers on Wednesday morning in the Wigwams, a series of rocky peaks on the west slope of the Teton mountain range, the Teton county coroner said. Investigators say it was likely he suffered a fatal fall. Standish had been attempting a thru-hike of the Continental Divide Trail between the Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks when he disappeared after contacting his family on 23 July, according to a statement from Teton county rescuers. Evidence suggests Standish may have fallen from a steep ridgeline that separates Grand Teton and the Jedediah Smith wilderness, officials said. Standish was discovered by a helicopter team after it spotted an orange backpack – and then saw his remains below the ridge. His family said it had stopped receiving updates from him via a Garmin GPS device and Facebook Messenger on 23 July, leading to a search being mounted by Teton county rescue crews. On 19 July, Standish gave an update from a location near Old Faithful, and described his planned route in the Tetons, Gros Ventre wilderness, the Wind River range, and the Divide Basin. Four days later, the family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message. There was also a Facebook Messenger video that they believe placed him in the Wigwams. The Teton county search and rescue team said it “sends its sincere condolences to the family and friends of the deceased”. It also expressed gratitude to federal agencies who assisted in searching for Standish. Standish had reportedly been following a popular thru-hike, or end-to-end through-hike, starting in Canada, the most northern point of the 3,100-mile Continental Divide Trail – which passes down through Montana, Idaho, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico. There have been other hiking-related deaths in North America recently. The Colorado Sun reported that a 15-year-old boy died after being struck by lightning on the state’s Mount Blue Sky on Monday. Sheriff’s officials identified the boy as Levi Strobel. Four other people were seriously injured, including Levi’s younger brother. In Arizona, a man died during a hike on Phoenix’s South Mountain. Richard Fletcher, 61, left his home early on Saturday morning. Investigators later said his death was consistent with a heat-related or medical event, authorities told local media. A 62-year-old man died in New Hampshire when he suffered a medical emergency in the state’s Welch-Dickey trail in the White Mountains. He was evacuated by national guard helicopter and later pronounced dead, according to New Hampshire Public Radio. Two hikers also died in Canada’s Banff national park. One was a woman in her 20s after falling from a mountain near Marvel Peak on Tuesday. Three days earlier, a 65-year-old from Calgary fell from Mount Temple, also in Banff, the CBC reported.

title: Middle East crisis live: Trump says ‘Israel is very happy’ with Gaza peace plan but doesn’t say if withdrawal or Hamas disarmament comes first
summary: The agreement is a ‘great breakthrough’, the president says in response to media questions
body: We are pausing this blog for the moment but our latest reporting can be found here: On Thursday night, Donald Trump declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces, issues that have so far stalled the implementation of last October’s ceasefire, but Israel has yet to respond officially to the plan and government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal. In particular, there is confusion over what should happen first, Hamas to disarm or the IDF to withdraw. Trump offered no clarity on the matter of the sequence of events at Friday’s cabinet meeting at Camp David. Asked if Israel was on board, Trump said: “We do have an understanding with Israel. Israel is very happy about it. They helped us and they’ve been very good about it.” There was also confusion over who Hamas would supposedly be handing over its heavy weapons too if the disarmament goes through – Trump said the Board of Peace, but officials announcing the deal said it would be Palestinian authorities. But at the time of writing, there has still been no confirmation from the Israeli government that it has accepted the agreement. Benjamin Netanyahu has yet to comment publicly, while his far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, on Friday dismissed the plan as “unacceptable”. An Israeli official also told Reuters: “Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the strip as a precondition for ‌any process.” They said the plan under discussion did not “provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections”. In similar vein, an Israeli source told AFP that Israel will not withdraw from the so-called Yellow Line in the Gaza Strip until Hamas undergoes “genuine disarmament”. Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, said “cosmetic solutions” wouldn’t work and Hamas had to “actually” disarm. He told CNN: “Disarmament means the weapons out of Gaza, they have no control of the weapons, and then we can move forward.” Hamas, meanwhile, has said it agreed to the roadmap on condition that disarmament was carried out at the same time as Israeli withdrawal. Indeed, the group released a statement saying it remains committed to negotiations on the next phase of the ceasefire, but insisted that Israel must commit to “halting the killing and ending its attacks” and that “handing over heavy weapons is also conditional on Israel ending hostilities and withdrawal from Gaza”. A member of the Hamas negotiating team, Ghazi Hamad, told Al Jazeera: “We will not take any action regarding disarmament prior to Israel’s withdrawal from the strip.” Hamad told Agence France-Presse in a separate interview: “The agreement contains a clear provision stating that Israel must commit to and implement its obligations. If Israel does not implement the agreement, neither will we.” Trump also said the US would be hitting Iran “very hard” when asked by reporters what Tehran can expect in the next few weeks. “At some point they’re going to say, ‘We just can’t take it anymore,’” he added. Trump also said he was “losing faith” in negotiations with Tehran, and implied, as he has done in the past, that Iranian negotiators were making him “angry” by saying one thing privately and another publicly. “They always want to talk, but they break their word so often … they just make me angry,” the US president said. “I’m losing faith in them because they do lie and do, they do misrepresent.” The Pentagon is considering reversing about half the staff cuts it made to a program dedicated to preventing wartime civilian casualties, the Atlantic reports, as the US military reckons with the human cost of its war against Iran – particularly the strike on a girls’ elementary school in Minab on the first day of the war that killed at least 168 people, most of them children. After US defence secretary Pete Hegseth fired or reassigned almost all of the staff working on the program, the potential reversal now awaits his signature, according to the magazine. Per the Atlantic’s report, “a Pentagon inspector-general report this spring found that the [US defence] department’s deep cuts in civilian-harm protections may have violated laws designed to safeguard noncombatants. Democrats are urging the department to reverse course. Hegseth’s comments and service history suggest that he will do otherwise. A Pentagon official – who, like other officials, spoke with us on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations – said in a statement that the setup for preventing civilian harm is ‘currently undergoing a strategic reassessment to inform its future reorganization’ and would remain in compliance with congressional requirements, but that no final decisions have been made.” The UN secretary general António Guterres has called the agreement for Hamas to give up its weapons and for Israel to withdraw from Gaza as “the only good news in recent days”. Speaking to reporters on Friday, he said: Let me be clear: the fighting must stop on all fronts in the region. We are now six months into the military escalation in the Gulf. What began as a regional conflict is increasingly becoming a driver of global instability.” A 10-year-old child has been shot in the back and injured by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, according to the official Palestinian news agency, Wafa. Local sources were reported to have said that live ammunition was used in the attack by settlers on a farm in the village of al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah. Lebanon’s president Joseph Aoun has called the Israeli army’s detonations near a 12th-century Unesco-listed castle (see 08.00 BST) a “direct threat” to a US-brokered deal between Beirut and Tel Aviv, according to Agence France-Presse. Aoun’s statement cited the country’s National Centre for Geophysics, saying that the explosions caused “ground waves equivalent to a 3.8 magnitude earthquake on the Richter scale”. He also raised concerns over the “negative messages” being sent ahead of planned talks in Rome between Lebanese and Israeli representatives. The explosions took place near Beaufort Castle, also known as Qalaat al-Shaqif, in parts of southern Lebanon that remain occupied by the Israeli military. Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, has said that Israel is “looking forward to implementing” the plan, but for it to work, Hamas must “actually” be willing to disarm, and that “cosmetic solutions” will not be enough for Israel. “We have to verify what they are doing, not what they are saying,” he said of Hamas in comments to CNN. Danon added said that the sequence of events surrounding disarmament, humanitarian aid and the IDF’s withdrawal from the so-called “yellow line” in Gaza could be discussed in future talks. Those issues we can discuss and we can resolve … you can build the sequence with the mediators. The main point is whether Hamas is actually willing to disarm or not. Because if they are playing games and offer cosmetic solutions, it will not work. Disarmament means the weapons out of Gaza, they have no control of the weapons, and then we can move forward. But Hamas told Reuters earlier that “the first step in executing the agreement is Israel’s commitment to stop killing and end violations [of the October ceasefire agreement]”. The group added that “handing over heavy weapons is also conditional on Israel ending hostilities and withdrawal from Gaza”. Asked if Trump should prepare to be disappointed by Israel’s willingness to engage with the peace plan, Danon said: “Absolutely not.” As we reported earlier, Trump failed to answer a question at his cabinet meeting about the sticking point of what should come first, Hamas’s disarmament or Israeli withdrawal from Gaza. Also at the cabinet meeting earlier, Donald Trump said he was “losing faith” in negotiations with Iran, and implied, as he has done in the past, that Iranian negotiators were making him “angry” by saying one thing privately and another publicly. They always want to talk, but they break their word so often. As an example, we’ll talk about nuclear, and we’ll be in there talking about nuclear for seven hours, and I say ... why do you need seven? You can take 10 minutes. You have five minutes, you should solve it. And they’ll go out and they’ll say, ‘We never discussed nuclear.’ And I say why, why do they say that? All they do is make me angry. You know, they just make me angry. He added: “I’m losing faith in them because they do lie and do, they do misrepresent.” Asked what he expects for Iran in the next few weeks, the US president said: “We’ll be hitting them very hard.” “You know, at some point they’re going to say, ‘We just can’t take it anymore,’” he added. Donald Trump has declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces, but Israeli government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal. In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to Julian Borger, the Guardian’s senior international correspondent. Trump’s secretary of state Marco Rubio hailed the Hamas disarmament deal is “another big step” towards achieving peace in the Middle East, and said it was “something a lot of people thought would never happen”. In his brief comments, Rubio also attacked the International Criminal Court, saying the court was “illegitimate”. Trump interjected with a joke to say that US efforts to dismantle the court were not aimed at defending him. “There’s no information that they are after me, [but] it could happen,” Trump joked. “[Marco] is trying to defend Bibi [Netanyahu] and various other people, but there are many people who shouldn’t be looked at that way. There is no indication that I’m one of them, at this moment.” A reminder that in November 2024, the ICC issued a warrant for the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gall…

title: Trump administration to let contract aiding unaccompanied minors expire
summary: US government, which owes legal services firm $65m, stopped paying in December, as contract runs out Friday
body: Current and former prosecutors are denouncing the Trump administration for fast-tracking the deportation of immigrant children, as a key contract for legal services is set to expire on Friday. A series of federal laws has for decades shielded child immigrants from removal, either to protect their safety or to allow them to testify against abusers or human traffickers. But the Trump administration has undermined those laws, immigrant advocates and prosecutors say, by directing immigration judges to fast-track deportation cases for minors and blocking their access to lawyers who might help them apply for several forms of relief from removal – including acting as witnesses in cases of human trafficking or domestic violence. “By arresting and deporting survivors who have come forward and applied for protection, the Administration not only risks endangering the survivor and their family members, but the Government also sends a chilling message to the larger community: don’t call the police, don’t report crime – you or your loved ones will get deported,” reads a Wednesday letter to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from 10 current and former prosecutors. “This undermines public safety for us all.” The lawyers sent the letter to the DHS the day before the Trump administration stands to let lapse a contract that pays for legal services to tens of thousands of unaccompanied minors. The Trump administration stopped paying the contract in December, according to the contractor, Acacia Center for Justice. The federal government owes Acacia roughly $65m. The Department of Health and Human Services, whose office of refugee resettlement is charged with caring for unaccompanied minors, has tried several times to establish a new contract for legal services, but those attempts have been blocked repeatedly through protests with the government accountability office, a spokesperson said. “The office of refugee resettlement works to ensure the safety, well-being, and appropriate care of all children in its custody,” HHS wrote in a written statement. “ORR remains fully compliant with its legal and regulatory obligations and does not act in any way that could dissuade a child from seeking appropriate legal relief.” “ORR offered Acacia the opportunity to receive a second bridge contract that included requirements to provide data on whom they represent and to bill the government when they submit applications for immigration relief,” the statement added. “Acacia declined that offer.” Stripping legal protections from unaccompanied minors threatens to both put them in harm’s way and make it easier for abusers to evade justice, said Maggy Krell, a California assembly member who worked on human-trafficking cases over her two-decade career as a prosecutor. “These crimes are vastly underreported, and now the government is setting up an additional barrier to threaten people with deportation if they have the courage to come forward,” said Krell, who signed the letter to the DHS. “It not only jeopardizes that person, it jeopardizes the entire prosecution. “Many of these kids are trafficking victims and they deserve protections in federal law, at a minimum,” she added. The Trump administration has been at odds with Acacia since last year, when HHS attempted to cancel the legal services contract to represent minors, only for a federal judge to order it reinstated later that year. Later, the Trump administration began pressing legal services providers to give up confidential information about clients. Legal services providers have refused to do so, contending that giving up such information could violate attorney-client privilege. Multiple lawsuits in federal court seek to force ORR to pay for legal services already given to unaccompanied minors. A hearing on the issue is slated for 6 August, according to Notus. But as the standoff draws on, legal providers have had little choice but to lay off or furlough lawyers who used to represent unaccompanied minors through the congressionally mandated program. Kids in Need of Defense, one of the legal non-profits that subcontracts with Acacia, announced last month that it will no longer work through the program, after racking up $20m in unpaid fees. Meanwhile, ICE has pushed more aggressively to deport unaccompanied minors. Immigration judges have issued roughly 10,000 removal and voluntary departure orders monthly against unaccompanied minors since Trump retook the White House, according to ProPublica – a figure about four times the rate from his first term. “These laws were enacted to protect survivors. What ICE is doing right now is completely upending that,” Krell said. “We’re talking about really traumatized kids here and other crime victims who are asking for help – and we’re locking them up and deporting them.”

title: ‘It ain’t the same’: inside the bitter battle to free Ben & Jerry’s
summary: Ben Cohen says his ice-cream company has been silenced by corporate ownership – and a boycott of Magnum brands could force a sale
body: Ben & Jerry’s ice-cream in the tub is still great, but the brand’s newest chocolate-covered ice-cream bar on a stick? “It ain’t the same,” Ben Cohen, the company co-founder, told the Guardian. Sure, the chocolate coating is still thick enough, but the ice cream itself is “kinda fluffy”, Cohen said – an insult in the ice-cream world that suggests extra air was added to cut costs. The criticism is surprising coming from Cohen, who opened his eponymous ice-cream shop in Burlington, Vermont, with childhood friend, Jerry Greenfield, in 1978. But it’s perhaps an apt metaphor of how he feels amid a simmering fight to take back Ben & Jerry’s from a parent company he says has silenced the brand’s trademark activism. For Cohen, 75, the battle is legal and existential. Ben & Jerry’s social and economic value was protected for decades, he says, by an independent board with final say on the brand’s voice, values and ice-cream quality. But that independence has all but disappeared, Cohen said. In November 2024, Ben & Jerry’s board sued parent company Unilever, claiming it was blocked from voicing support for Gaza, and accusing Unilever of breaching their agreement. The lawsuit is still making its way through federal court. In September 2025, after Unilever said it would spin off its ice-cream brands into the Magnum Ice Cream Company, Cohen started his campaign to “Free Ben & Jerry’s” – asking Magnum to sell the brand so it can be independently owned and operated. Social activism is a core part of why people buy Ben & Jerry’s, Cohen says. “What consumers want above all is authenticity and attitude,” he said. Ben & Jerry’s could be valued at $1bn or more, Cohen estimates, but says Magnum won’t give him or potential investors numbers that could help value it more accurately. Magnum has insisted Ben & Jerry’s is not up for sale, so Cohen is amping up his campaign. In recent weeks, Cohen has started calling for a boycott of Magnum’s other brands, including Yasso, Breyers, Talenti and Klondike, with the idea that tanking the company’s overall sales will pressure it to sell back the company. “We didn’t want it to have to come to this,” he said of the boycott, but Magnum is “destroying a brand” that stands for values its customers believe in. What Cohen is trying to do – force an $11bn conglomerate into divesting a star brand – is highly unusual, and unlikely to succeed, some industry and management experts predict. “Most boycotts fail because people get distracted,” said Maurice Schweitzer, a management professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. US and European consumers just may not have the long-term attention span for the sustained collective action that it would take to pressure management, Schweitzer said. But Cohen believes the company’s loyal followers are on his side. “Consumers want to vote with their dollars,” he said, insisting that support for the brand must continue. “We want Ben & Jerry’s to remain strong because we plan on eventually owning it.” The flavors of conflict It’s been nearly three decades since Cohen and Greenfield sold their company to Unilever for $326m in 2000. The unique deal was built around an independent board and lauded by the Wharton School for preserving the company’s pledge to try to “make the world a better place” while also committing to making great ice-cream and turning a profit. Under Unilever, Ben & Jerry’s was vocally supportive of social issues. The company criticized George W Bush’s war in Iraq, was a pioneering supporter of same-sex marriage, and called to “dismantle white supremacy” after George Floyd was murdered. But now, the divide between the brand’s founders and the company’s corporate owners is deep and bitter. Cracks first opened after an independent board overseeing the company said in 2021 that selling Ben & Jerry’s ice cream in occupied Palestine was “inconsistent with our values”, sparking outrage in Israel. Unilever sold off the Israeli trademark to a local businessman who is now selling a “Milk & Honey” flavor. The board first sued Unilever in 2024, accusing the company of silencing its activism over Palestine, including vocal support for Gaza and calls to stop US aid to Israel. Then in 2025, Unilever ousted David Stever, the Ben & Jerry’s CEO, in a move Ben & Jerry’s said was designed to stifle its social mission, including a board-approved plan to sell a watermelon flavor to support Palestine that was quashed. In a statement to the Guardian, Unilever said Stever’s role was re-evaluated because of the spinoff, not the social mission, and that he turned down a role in the larger company and chose to quit. Co-founder Greenfield quit soon after, stepping away from the company for the first time in 50 years, saying it had lost its independence. Currently, the board has just two Unilever veterans after Magnum imposed new term limits. Though the campaign to buy back Ben & Jerry’s has been led by Cohen, Greenfield said in his resignation letter that leaving the board was one of the “hardest and most painful decisions” he had ever made. “It is profoundly disappointing to come to the conclusion that that independence, the very basis of our sale to Unilever, is gone,” he said. “If the company couldn’t stand up for the things we believed, then it wasn’t worth being a company at all.” Earlier in July, Ben & Jerry’s philanthropic foundation said it was forced to close after Magnum cut its funding. Magnum says an investigation found “governance and conflict-of-interest issues”. In an interview with the Guardian, Magnum’s chief corporate affairs and sustainability officer Victoria McKenzie-Gould said it invited trustees of the foundation to partner on a stronger corporate governance framework, but they declined. “Our focus remains where it belongs: on supporting the Ben & Jerry’s team and its three-part mission while making great ice-cream and campaigning on the causes the brand cares about – and the team is doing a fantastic job,” McKenzie-Gould said. ‘Not for sale’ Throughout Cohen’s months-long fight to buy back his company, Magnum has said it has no intention of selling. “Ben is a great campaigner, but Ben & Jerry’s is not for sale, and we are confident in the future because Ben & Jerry’s is thriving as part of the Magnum Ice Cream Company,” McKenzie-Gould said. Magnum doesn’t break out sales by brand, but called Ben & Jerry’s one of its “top four”, with 3% organic sales growth in 2025; about 35% of Magnum’s €7.9bn ($9.1bn) 2025 revenue came from the Americas, traditionally Ben & Jerry’s largest market. Sales grew 9.2% in the second quarter, “powered by innovation”, Ben & Jerry’s CEO, Jochanan Senf, said on Thursday, adding that all three parts of the company’s mission – social, product and economic – must “thrive equally in a way that commands deep respect for individuals in and outside the company”. Since it was acquired in 2000, Ben & Jerry’s “footprint has grown from four to over 40 countries, [and] revenue has grown more than fivefold,” McKenzie-Gould said. The company’s overall social mission has received €500m ($576m) from the parent – more than the original purchase price. The brand had spoken out recently on “ICE; refugee support in Europe; cannabis justice and voting rights”, a corporate spokesperson for the Ben & Jerry’s brand told the Guardian, including a new flavor – Razz Up! – that encourages midterm voting. The spokesperson disagreed with Cohen’s criticism of the new ice-cream bars, saying the product was approved by the independent board in 2024 and used the same design standards as every product. “More than one-third of bar buyers in the last year are completely new fans to Ben & Jerry’s,” Senf said with second-quarter results. Cohen’s calls for a boycott comes as many Americans are angry at companies and frustrated over US policies. American support for Palestinians and criticism of Donald Trump have grown, and there’s a growing frustration with big companies over shoddy products and bad service. But the headwinds for a successful boycott are stiff. There’s a war against “woke capitalism”, and shareholder support for environmental, social and governance resolutions has plummeted. Many of the social media platforms Cohen needs to spread his message are controlled by conservative billionaires, leaving him at the mercy of their algorithms. “I do think this is going to get lost in the shuffle of so many other causes,” said Schweitzer. Plenty of fans seem to think Cohen’s expectations are naive. “Did you really think a giant company wouldn’t exploit you? When has an international company ever had social values?” wrote Base_Art, a painter, on Instagram. But Cohen has also gathered about 200,000 signatures and lots of encouraging social media messages. “Occasionally, I ate the vegan coffee Talenti,” former model Christie Brinkley recently wrote on Instagram. But without an independent board of directors, she said: “No more!” Cohen acknowledges the hurdles, but says he believes longtime, loyal fans will help overcome them. “I think that there’s millions of people who support Ben and Jerry’s and support its social mission,” Cohen said. “I’m going to take it until we win.”

title: Trump backtracks from promise to let Ukraine build Patriot missiles
summary: US president tells reporters during Camp David cabinet meeting technology ‘a hard thing to give away’
body: Donald Trump has backed off a promise to let Ukraine manufacture its own Patriot air defense interceptors, telling reporters that handing over the underlying technology was “a hard thing to give away” during a cabinet meeting at Camp David. The retreat, billed by the White House as “something different” for the cabinet to experience together, was the first such meeting at the presidential compound of Trump’s second term. It also became the venue for the US president to unpick, in real time, a commitment he made to Volodymyr Zelenskyy just a few days earlier. Asked whether he was ready to grant Kyiv a license to build Patriots domestically – something he had suggested at a Nato summit in Turkey just this month, and which the Ukrainian president described as a productive topic in their White House meeting on Tuesday – Trump was noncommittal. “We have not agreed to that,” he said. “We’re talking about it, but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology.” Giving away the weapons carried its own risks, he added: “People that you give that technology, they can some day turn on you. You know that is possible.” The interceptor travels at “8,600 miles an hour”, Trump explained, adding for context: “If you go 60, it gets to be a little fast.” He went on to recall an occasion on which five missiles were fired “at Jordan” and were shot down in sequence – rendered by the president as “bing bing bing bing”. “Nobody else has that capacity,” he said of the system, before concluding that Washington “will be building many plants” to produce Patriots and Tomahawk missiles domestically – just not, for now, in Ukraine. The reversal is likely to unsettle Kyiv, which has spent the past year lobbying for both more interceptors and the means to produce its own, amid a global shortage that has been compounded by the volume of Patriot and Tomahawk stock expended in Washington’s confrontation with Iran. Trump touched on that conflict too, telling reporters the US would be “hitting them very hard” if talks broke down, and dismissing Iran’s military as effectively hollowed out. “They have no navy … they have no anti-aircraft,” he complained, comparing the controversial five-month campaign favorably with US wars in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Korea, and arguing in each case that the war lasted “many years”, whereas his administration had achieved more, in less time. His stated goals for the campaign have repeatedly shifted. An expert analysis of the Pentagon’s own arsenals tell a different story: the Center for Strategic and International Studies says two-thirds of the department’s Patriot interceptors have been used, perhaps prompting a $58.6bn army contract with Lockheed Martin to rebuild supplies, along with a recent White House request to Congress for tens of billions of dollars more in emergency funding. The Camp David gathering came a day after Trump announced what he called a “historic” agreement for Hamas to disarm and for Israeli forces to withdraw from Gaza, a claim that has yet to be confirmed by Israel. Pressed on the sequencing of the deal – whether disarmament or withdrawal would come first, the issue that has stalled negotiations for months – Trump declined to specify either way, saying only that Washington had “an understanding” with Israel and that the Israelis were “very happy about it”. He was similarly light on detail when asked if the agreement would actually hold, despite a diplomatic backdrop that includes an outstanding international criminal court (ICC) arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, an unresolved international court of justice (ICJ) case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, arms restrictions imposed by several governments over the conduct of the war, and a governing coalition at home that has repeatedly rejected anything short of Hamas’s total disarmament before any withdrawal. “The people are very complex and difficult,” said Trump. “In many cases wonderful, in many cases not so wonderful.” An Israeli official has said that no withdrawal from the so-called Yellow Line will happen before Hamas fully disarms, while members of Netanyahu’s own coalition have voiced opposition to the plan, details Trump did not address.

title: At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco
summary: Pedro Sánchez decries ‘violation of territorial integrity’ as other EU countries criticise Madrid over incident
body: At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a mixed reaction from other EU countries, including calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Sánchez, who arrived in Ceuta on Friday morning, said he would use all the resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the city’s population. He attributed the mass crossing to “human trafficking mafias” that had taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta, or Spain’s other north African enclave of Melilla, could not be summarily returned under special rules. Sánchez said: “That has spread like wildfire during these last few hours through the networks of mafias that traffic in human beings and has produced an avalanche of the characteristics and dimension that we experienced yesterday.” Sánchez said a temporary reception centre would be established to facilitate the documentation, registration, triage and “expedited” expulsion of people with no legal claim to be in Spain. He also said the government would erect a visible barrier – a line of buoys – near the breakwater at Ceuta’s Tarajal beach to make it clear where the border was, and to legally comply with the court’s ruling. Although the Spanish government said about 50,000 people had crossed the border on Thursday and in the early hours of Friday, the president of Ceuta put the figure at about 60,000. Spain’s interior ministry, which has deployed additional police officers and soldiers to the enclave, said more than 48,300 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday. The Irish presidency of the EU has convened a meeting of member states on Saturday, under the Integrated Political Crisis Response mechanism. EU sources said this will provide experts from member states with an opportunity “to discuss the movements into Ceuta over the last two days, the numbers of people who have returned to Morocco today, the supports being provided by the EU to Spain and diplomatic engagement with Morocco”. A further meeting of EU ambassadors has been called in Brussels on Monday. The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over the course of two days. That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania. That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group. Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria. Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”. Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich, was quoted by the Associated Press as saying that “we have always prioritized legal, orderly and safe migration for all” and indicated that the situation had developed against Rabat’s wishes. Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers’ association representing officers of the Spanish Guardia Civil – which patrols Spain’s borders – described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. Without shelter, thousands of people, including unaccompanied children, had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements, while others roamed the streets aimlessly. “It’s chaotic,” said Sbihi. Among those who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said. Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children. Ceuta and Melilla have the EU’s only land border with Africa. ‌Both cities periodically experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe. The events in Ceuta led some EU countries to issue strong threats or rebukes. Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”. Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”. Italy announced on Friday evening that it would be suspending its Schengen arrangements with Spain, but the practical impact of the move was not immediately clear. Meloni said the measure would be kept in force only as long as needed, adding: “In parallel, Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.” Responding to Italy’s unilateral decision, a European Commission spokesperson said a member state “may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security”. But they added that the member state would need to notify the commission and explain how the situation in Ceuta constituted such a threat. The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of its EU partners of its decision. The Swedish prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, urged Spain to “act swiftly to regain control of the situation and fulfil its commitments within Schengen cooperation”. The Finnish interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said that as Spain had “completely failed to protect the Schengen area’s external border”, all EU countries should support Italy’s proposal to suspend its Schengen status. However, in a statement later on Friday, the European Commission said Ceuta and Melilla were subject to special Schengen rules that prevented onward movement within the zone. The EU’s migration commissioner, Magnus Brunner, called the situation in Ceuta “unacceptable” and said he was in close contact with the Spanish authorities. But he also confirmed there was no onward route from Ceuta given the enclave’s unique status under the Schengen rules. He said: “The Schengen borders code provides for special rules that apply to Ceuta and Melilla. Border checks on persons departing from Ceuta and Melilla remain in force.” But there were also shows of unity. The European Council president, António Costa, expressed his “solidarity with Spain in the current situation of illegal migration in Ceuta”. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and to offer assistance to Spain. But, as a precautionary measure, Macron said he had asked the interior ministry to strengthen the French controls on its border with Spain with four mobile units and drones. In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) called on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient. In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.” The far-right Vox party called the incident “an invasion”. On Friday evening, hundreds attended an anti-migrant rally outside the Moroccan embassy in Madrid, with images showing some protesters performing Nazi salutes and waving flags with far-right insignia.

title: Italy says it’s temporarily suspending EU Schengen arrangement with Spain after 60,000 migrants reach Ceuta – as it happened
summary: The measure will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries
body: Just as we closed the blog, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni has confirmed the move to suspend the free movement with on air and sea borders with Spain. She said it was “an extraordinary measure, adopted to safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation.” In another sign that it may stop short of full border control for all arrivals from Spain (19:19), she said “the measure will be kept in force only for the time necessary, with particular attention to limiting any impact on summer tourist flows.” She added that “Italy is ready to support every European initiative to assist Spanish institutions as needed to restore full control of the Union’s external borders and to address the ongoing situation with determination.” “Defending borders means defending the safety of citizens, combating irregular immigration, and striking at the criminal networks that traffic human beings,” she said. And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today. At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 60,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco (17:33). Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called it a “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity” (12:51) and blamed on misleading narratives spread by human traffickers (12:54, 13:17). In response, Italy has moved to suspend its free-travel Schengen arrangements with Spain by sea and air (18:26), claiming it was necessary to safeguard the security of its citizens (19:02, 19:07). It is understood it will amount to “targeted, selective checks” on third-country nationals arriving from Spain (19:19). But by Friday afternoon, the Spanish authorities claimed that a vast majority of the migrants have voluntarily returned to Morocco (16:41, 18:20), with hundreds more going back by the hour as there was no onwards migration route to mainland Spain or the EU (14:02, 15:04). The huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to a barrage of criticism from the US (15:25, 15:29, 18:02) and other EU countries, including broader calls to suspend Spain’s membership of the Schengen area (9:42, 10:21, 12:10, 13:52, 14:52, 16:59, 17:38). If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com. I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa. Spain found an unexpected ally in Slovakia’s Robert Fico, who said that he did not believe that “excluding Spain from the Schengen Area would be the right solution” as he offered help to the government in Madrid. In a lengthy post in English, he said: “I am closely monitoring developments in the migration crisis in the Spanish enclave in Africa on an hourly basis. Today, I also joined the initiative of Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni calling for a strong response from the EU institutions. The Government of the Slovak Republic has long maintained that the most effective way to prevent illegal migration is the rigorous protection of the Schengen external borders. In other words, everything possible – and even what may seem impossible – must be done to prevent illegal migrants from entering the territory of EU Member States without authorisation. It is striking to observe the hypocrisy of many EU Member States, as well as EU representatives, who only a few years ago, through their lax approach, allowed illegal migrants to enter EU countries in massive numbers, causing serious crises. Today, everyone presents themselves as a determined opponent of illegal migration, having seen how voters across individual Member States politically removed several governments because of their inability to deal with the migration crisis. I would like to recall that, several years ago, when I exercised my right of veto and prevented the adoption of mandatory migrant quotas at the European Council, I had to endure considerable political hostility and criticism. Radical, even extreme, proposals will also emerge in connection with the current crisis in Africa. As prime minister of the Slovak Republic, I do not believe that excluding Spain from the Schengen Area would be the right solution. Just as we were prepared to assist France in combating wildfires, Slovakia should also adhere to its proven strategy of protecting the Schengen external borders at all costs. Any country requiring assistance in safeguarding those borders should receive the maximum possible support through the deployment of police officers and the technical equipment necessary for border protection. Slovakia is ready to offer such assistance to Spain.” It looks like not everyone is Italy sees the need to adopt these measures. As Reuters noted, Meloni’s coalition, which came to power in 2022 promising to reduce illegal immigration, has faced strong pressure from a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci, whose anti-migrant rhetoric has resonated with some voters. “The problem is that this is ⁠a purely demagogic proposal, as usual designed for domestic consumption and to compete with Vannacci, without solving anything at all,” said Piero De Luca, a senior lawmaker with the centre-left Democratic Party. We are getting a bit more detail on what the Italian decision will mean in practice. The Italian interior ministry said border police would carry out “targeted, selective checks” on third-country nationals arriving from Spain to verify that they had the documents needed for travel within the European Union, Reuters reported. Remember that it’s all a bit symbolic – or political – as all people leaving Ceuta still have to go through a Spanish border control anyway, and do not have free access to the EU or the Schengen zone, as per the EU’s rules (14:02), As mentioned earlier, the issue of migration has become heavily toxic in domestic politics of many countries (14:02), so it may or may not be relevant to just mention in passing that Italy is expected to go to the polls at some point next year – with some media reports suggesting that it could happen as early as April 2027. Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani has just confirmed the decision to close Italy’s air and sea borders with Spain. In a post on X, he said the temporary suspension of Schengen with Spain “is a necessary choice to safeguard the security of our citizens and defend the European borders.” He stressed that it was “a measure provided for by the treaties and made unavoidable today.” “The migrant crisis in Ceuta reminds us that the management of the Union’s borders is a shared responsibility among our countries, one toward the other. We must work together to prevent uncontrolled migrant flows from entering EU territory, with all the consequent risks and the threat of terrorism, which must be confronted without hesitation.” For what it’s worth, Italy’s reported decision to close borders with Spain follows a specific and direct suggestion they could do just that. As reported this morning (9:42), prime minister Giorgia Meloni said last night that “Italy will not stand by and watch,” and suggested it was “prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain.” In the absence of a detailed breakdown of the proposed measures from the Italian government, I managed to get a bit more from the European Commission on what are the legal options available to Rome. A commission spokesperson crucially insisted that “there are today no onward movements from Cueta,” with the focus on “getting the situation under control and making sure people are returning to Morocco.” But they added that: “For the general legal framework, the rules provide that Member States may exceptionally and temporarily reintroduce internal border control as a matter of last resort, to address serious threats to public order or national security (Article 25(1)(c)) Where such threat is unforeseeable and requires immediate action, the Member State may, on an exceptional basis, immediately reintroduce border control at internal borders. The Member State in question would need to notify the Commission, Council, Parliament and other Member States thereof and explain how the situation in Ceuta constitutes a serious threat to their public policy or internal security. As regards maritime travel: What is possible is a reintroduction of internal border control at the internal sea borders. However Article 41 of the Schengen Borders Code provides that the special rules applicable to Ceuta and Melilla remain in place, meaning there is border control between Ceuta and Melilla and the rest of the Schengen area.” The Guardian understands that Italy has not yet formally notified any of the partners of its decision, which may explain why we don’t know the details of the proposed measures yet. There are some precedents: for example, Germany has reinstated some border controls with its neighbours in 2024 as a measure against irregular migration. The latest set of measures is due to expire in September, but German ministers suggested today it would be extended once again. Just like Reuters (18:26), the Italian news agency Ansa says the Italian ministry of interior “has ordered the closure of the sea and air borders with Spain.” It adds that “the decision was made following the most recent information were analysed by the Committee on Immigration and Border Security,” chaired by the interior minister, Matteo Piantedosi. But there are no further details available at this stage. Meanwhile, ever a diplomat, France’s Emmanuel Macron said he had been in touch with the Spanish government to express his solidarity and offer assistance to Spain. “I welcome the ongoing cooperation with Morocco, which has already enabled more than 40,000 returns from Ceuta to Morocco today.
