title: Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling
summary: Labour MPs fear No 10 team lack up-to-date energy insight and don’t fully recognise voters’ climate concerns
body: Andy Burnham was told he could face the first revolt of his premiership as Labour MPs and climate experts condemned his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas. As the UK suffers through drought, fires and heatwaves, the prime minister gave the strongest indication yet on Friday he was minded to allow new drilling. His comments came just hours before the UN secretary-general warned “every new fossil fuel project” made heatwaves more dangerous. Speaking at a community centre in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham repeated he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas and that decisions on new drilling would be made “in due course”. But he added: “The question isn’t whether Britain will still be using oil and gas, the question is where does it come from.” But many Labour MPs are increasingly worried about how support for expanded drilling will play with an electorate alarmed by the worst drought since 1976, soaring temperatures, wildfires, and climate-related food inflation and potential supply shortages. They worry about losing more voters to the Greens: Zack Polanski’s party has stressed its opposition to further new licences for the North Sea, including the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea and the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland. A decision to go ahead with the projects could trigger a new surge in defectors from Labour. Rachael Maskell, the Labour MP for York Central, urged ministers to “keep carbon in the ground”, and watch the recent national emergency climate briefing. She added: “We’re seeing ice caps melting, seas warming up, hotter and hotter summers. This summer has been a warning that we have to go towards a sustainable future fast.” Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, said there was “no legitimate reason” to press ahead with Jackdaw because it would make only a negligible difference to energy prices while sending the wrong signal internationally as Europe experienced record heat. Lewis said approving the field would show Burnham was “not looking at the evidence” and that Labour risked adding “the stain of the climate crisis” to the party’s record, alongside Gaza. Chris Murray, the Labour MP for Edinburgh East and Musselburgh, said the UK must stay the course on decarbonisation. “Britain was the first country to industrialise and we have a duty to lead the world on net zero. We must be wary of the self-interest from which oil and gas companies are arguing, while the future of the planet is at stake.” António Guterres, the UN secretary-general, did not single out the UK but gave a pointed warning on Friday, as the World Meteorological Organisation forecast hotter temperatures from August to October. “Every new fossil fuel project approved today makes tomorrow’s heatwaves more dangerous, and our world less secure,” Guterres said. “Yet some governments still plan to produce more than twice as much fossil fuel in 2030 as the 1.5-degree limit allows. More coal, oil and gas will lead to a more combustible future.” These warnings are hitting home with voters, several Labour MPs told the Guardian. One source said “there will be a revolt” if there is a chance for Labour MPs to vote on new licences for the North Sea. Jackdaw and Rosebank are already in the planning system, and so could be argued to fall outside Labour’s manifesto promise to halt new licensing. Despite these loopholes, the source said Burnham would need “support from the Conservatives and possibly the SNP rather than Labour unity” if it came to a vote, though Burnham is likely to try to avoid this by taking any decisions as an administrative measure after consultations on the fields conclude in mid-August. Concerns over the negative impact of allowing new North Sea drilling extend across the Labour party, transcending factions and “tribes”. The Guardian has contacted or been told of concerned MPs including ministers and junior members of government, longstanding senior backbench MPs and committee figures and new MPs from the 2024 general election intake. A decision on Rosebank and Jackdaw will not come before the consultations end in mid-August, but the issue of whether further drilling could be allowed is likely to still be live when the budget comes on 28 October. In a video message on social media on Friday announcing the date, the chancellor, John Healey, said it would be “a budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain”, and that it would be “built on fiscal discipline”. Part of the North Sea problem, according to some insiders, is that Burnham has assembled an older economic team with traditional views on industry, lacking knowledge of the climate and the rapidly changing dynamics of energy around the world. Several influential economists told the Guardian that increased drilling would not help the UK economy. Mariana Mazzucato, who worked closely with Burnham on the lauded transformation of transport in Manchester, and who has been a key influence on his thinking, said: “Drilling the North Sea won’t help people across the UK struggling with their energy bills – most of the oil and gas from these new sites would be sold to the highest bidder on international markets. “But the bigger picture is that green industrial strategy requires coherent and credible policy signals, to give investors confidence that the ‘clean energy superpower’ mission of Labour’s manifesto is still the direction of travel – which this drilling would undermine.” Daniela Gabor, a professor of economics at SOAS, added: “It’s a terrible idea. The Burnham government is caving to the fossil lobby just as we experience some of the most intense heatwaves of recent times.” Nicholas Stern, the economist, said new drilling would not alleviate pressure on energy bills and dismissed arguments that UK North Sea oil would lead to fewer carbon emissions than imports. “Extra output leads to extra use and more greenhouse gases. Further, and importantly, it would send a dangerous signal to the world,” he said. However, some backbench MPs are also wary of the “massive bear trap”, as one described it, of allowing the climate to become a wedge issue for voters, as the Tories and Reform party are seeking to do. They are prepared to keep the peace by accepting the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield, and potentially even the more controversial Rosebank oilfield, if a line can then be drawn against any further licences and if Burnham reaffirms his commitment to pushing forward urgently with net zero. That is still in question. “[There is] growing concern among MPs that No 10 don’t realise this [new drilling] won’t help with bills at all and will cause political damage,” said another Labour backbencher. “A pragmatic approach can help us navigate this but the fundamentals need to be understood.”

title: Water cuts loom as US unveils long-awaited response to Colorado river crisis
summary: Federal government plan outlines cuts to California, Arizona and Nevada but fix is likely to be only temporary
body: The US government released its anxiously awaited plan for how to manage the Colorado river crisis on Friday, outlining cuts in water supplied to California, Arizona and Nevada. The proposal from the US Bureau of Reclamation spares Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming from facing mandatory cuts, for now. But it is a temporary fix as the states that rely on the river continue to fight over a long-term management plan for the dwindling resource that supplies huge swaths of the western US. The proposal is the federal government’s answer to a years-long stalemate between the seven states responsible for forming a plan on how to distribute the deep cuts needed to pull the system back from the brink. It comes just months before the framework that currently governs the essential and imperiled waterway is set to expire. “This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the Basin States to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions,” said Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, in a press release. Under the 10-year plan, the Lower Basin states could face deep cuts of up to 3m acre-feet (3.7bn kiloliters) a year – up to 40% of their collective total – “subject to hydrology”, according to the press release by the Department of the Interior. That’s about enough water annually to serve more than 25 million people. The plan would also allow annual releases of between 5m and 12m acre-feet from Lake Powell, the basin’s second-largest reservoir. Under the 10-year federal framework, water management decisions will be made every two years. The federal government is expected to release a record of decision in the coming week that will detail operations under the plan in the short term, but it is likely they will closely follow a proposal issued by the lower basin states earlier this year that would shave 3.2m acre-feet from their combined total over 2027 and 2028. Governing the enormous and essential river system has always been deeply challenging. The federal government has limited jurisdiction over water policies and agreements between states. A century-old compact that initially divided up the river gave rights to more water than there is in the system. With the river’s decline, the gap has only widened. The combined levels of the two largest reservoirs on the river, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have already reached record lows and it’s exceedingly unlikely that the system will bounce back, even if there is a wet winter. The Bureau of Reclamation has the power to manage operations of the dams at the two central reservoirs, which provide hydroelectric power and supply the flows from the upper states to the lower, which is largely why, experts say, the cuts were directed at the lower basin states. The river and its tributaries are the lifeblood for the American west, supplying bustling cities such as Las Vegas, Phoenix and Los Angeles, as well as agricultural centers. Roughly 40 million people in seven states, two countries and dozens of tribes rely on the river, which also irrigates 5.5m acres of farmland. The Colorado has been overdrawn for more than a century, as demand continues to outpace supply. The climate crisis is also taking an increasingly large share. Snowmelt that feeds the river is evaporating more quickly, and thirsty soils and plants soak up more water. Flows in the Colorado are down 20% over the last century and precipitation has shrunk by about 7%. Snaking across 1,450 miles (2,300km) from the Rocky Mountains into Mexico, the sprawling basin fuels an estimated $1.4tn in economic activity and is also home to scores of birds, fish, plants and animals, its diverse ecosystems providing critical habitat for more than 150 threatened or endangered species. The ecosystems on the banks of the river have already paid a heavy price. Fourteen native fish species are endangered or threatened. The once-lush wetlands in Mexico’s river delta have been dry for decades and the once mighty river slows to just a trickle as it crosses the US-Mexico border. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Wait goes on for result in Greater Manchester mayoral by-election – as it happened
summary: The turnout was recorded as the lowest on record for a mayoral role in the region
body: As we await the results of the first round of the Greater Manchester mayoral by-election, here is a summary of some of the main political developments today: The chancellor, John Healey, has confirmed that the autumn budget will be delivered on 28 October Healey emphasised the need for “fiscal credibility” and said that the Treasury would “abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East”. Elsewhere: The PM has backed stronger regulation of the funeral home sector after the jailing of a disgraced funeral boss Planning permission for a Chinese “super-embassy” has been upheld at the High Court after a challenge from a residents’ association was dismissed Labour’s former deputy leader Harriet Harman has suggested that men should be banned from running to become the party’s next leader For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog. The count is still ongoing at the Co-op Live arena in Manchester, as we await a result from the first preference voting. In the meantime, here are some photos for those of you that enjoy seeing the democratic process in action… It was reported earlier that Andy Burnham has indicated he could drop a plan to restrict jury trials. During Keir Starmer’s premiership, ministers unveiled a proposal to reserve jury trials for the most serious cases such as murder and rape and offences with a likely sentence of more than three years in prison. Now Mark Evans, president of the Law Society of England and Wales, has called for the government to “move quickly to set out a comprehensive, whole-system plan” to address court backlogs, warning the system was “under immense pressure”. He added: This should include sustained investment in people, infrastructure and technology. Any efforts to reduce court backlogs must not come at the expense of fundamental safeguards. Jury trials must be protected to ensure public confidence in our justice system. Sky News is reporting that there is “slow progress” being made in the count at the Co-Op Arena, Manchester. If no one candidate secures 50% of the vote, it will go to a second round of voting – which means it will be a late one. All recent polling suggest Labour’s Bev Craig will win the highest number of votes but not 50%. But, given that the Greens will likely be eliminated in third place, most second preference votes under this system seem likely to switch to Labour, rather than Reform. The Manchester Evening News is reporting that the first round result from the Greater Manchester mayoral election will come in at about 4pm. Stick with us as we are monitoring for any breaking updates. Andy Burnham has indicated he will scrap plans to curtail jury trials in England and Wales, abandoning one of the most significant overhauls from Keir Starmer’s government. The prime minister said he had concerns about the proposals and that his instinct was to keep juries at the heart of the justice system. Speaking at a community centre in Sheffield on Friday, Burnham said he was reluctant to do away with jury trials due to his experience campaigning for justice over the Hillsborough disaster. “I have my concerns about the plan to restrict a jury trial, partly from my personal experience, particularly in Hillsborough,” he said. “So I want to really look in detail at that proposal, and my instincts are that we need to find ways of not reducing access to jury trial.” You can read the full story here: The chancellor, John Healey, said he will deliver his first budget on 28 October, which he promises will meet Labour’s existing “fiscal rules” and “give businesses and families some of the stability they need to plan for the future”. Healey wrote to the chair of the Treasury committee, Meg Hillier, to confirm the date. “This will be a Budget that moves power and money out of Westminster, into every postcode in Britain,” the former defence secretary wrote. “Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security. That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East.” Healey will need to make tough choices and reveal details about how he will fund the government’s latest policy announcements, including cuts to VAT on electricity bills and business rates for pubs, as well as commitments to increase defence spending. He took up his position at a time of soaring energy prices from the US-Israel war on Iran, inflationary pressures and sluggish growth across the UK economy. The Guardian’s north of England editor, Josh Halliday, has looked into Labour’s expected electoral fortunes in the Greater Manchester mayoral byelection race – and how the voting system could work in the party’s favour. Here is an extract from his analysis piece: The byelection is taking place under the supplementary voting system, which means that if no single party achieves 50% then second-choice preferences will come into play. Labour is widely seen as having an advantage under this system as it is more likely to be picked as the second choice for Green, Lib Dem and even some Conservative voters. Reform UK, by contrast, cannot count on such broad support. The More in Common poll found that Labour’s lead would stretch to 30 points if Reform UK finished second, as Craig is the most popular second choice for most Greens and a sizeable chunk of Conservatives. Anything short of a strong second-place finish would be a blow to Reform UK, which won more than 100 seats in Greater Manchester in the May elections, including all but one of the 25 up for grabs in Wigan – the council of Burnham’s new constituency – and 18 out of 19 in Tameside, both once solidly Labour areas. One senior Labour figure said the party expected to do much better in these areas in the mayoral byelection, having won back voters who backed Reform UK only two months ago in what many saw as a protest vote against Keir Starmer. Counting is under way in the byelection to choose Andy Burnham’s successor as Greater Manchester mayor. Polling stations closed at 22:00pm last night, with the count taking place from 09:00am this morning. We are expecting a result early this afternoon. As of 14.05pm on Friday, the turnout was revealed as being 25.14%, with 538,659 votes cast from an electorate of more than two million people. The turnout was the lowest on record for a mayoral role in the region, reflecting widespread voter apathy and disillusion with politcians. At the 2024 election, the turnout was 32%, in 2021 it was 34% and about 28% in 2017 when the first Greater Manchester mayoral election took place. The contest was triggered by Burnham’s election to parliament last month, after he was elected as the new MP for Makerfield on 18 June, winning 55% of the historic vote. Polling ahead of Thursday’s vote suggested Labour candidate Bev Craig, the leader of Manchester city council, was on course to win by a comfortable margin. Her main rival is likely to be either Reform UK’s Sian Astley or the Green party’s Geraldine Coggins. Other candidates were Phil Eckersley (Conservatives), Richard Kilpatrick (Lib Dems), Marlon West (Restore Britain) and Marcus Farmer (Independent). The government has announced a crack down on rogue funeral operators in order to better protect bereaved families after Robert Bush’s sentencing. The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) will work alongside other departments, including the Ministry of Justice, to develop proposals to improve regulatory standards in the funeral sector. In a press release, the DHSC said: As part of this work, the Law Commission will undertake a review of the criminal law in relation to the deceased, consider any gaps in existing legal protections and make recommendations on the creation of new offences, if they are needed. For bereaved families, there can be few things more painful than knowing a loved one was not treated properly after they died. The deceased cannot speak for themselves, which is why clear safeguards, stronger oversight and consistent standards are needed to protect their dignity and give families the reassurance they deserve. During a visit to Sheffield on Friday, the prime minister said he backed the regulation of funeral homes and mortuaries as he extended his sympathies to the families of victims of the disgraced funeral director Robert Bush, who was jailed for 20 years this afternoon for offences carried out at his business, Legacy Independent Funeral Directors. “I do back those calls, and there were recommendations in the Fuller Report that will be implemented because we have seen appalling situations like this before,” Burnham said, in reference to the official inquiry into the double killer David Fuller, who was found to have abused more than 100 bodies in an NHS mortuary over a 12-year period. “I feel for the families and I know it’ll be a difficult day for them with these matters in court again,” the prime minister added. “I was truly horrified when I heard what had happened. Appalling for any family to go through that. This needs a proper response in terms of the regulation needed, to make sure no family goes through that again.” “People, I think, would assume that the highest standards apply to this area and we’ve got to make sure that they do apply and that there can’t be any repeat of what we’ve seen.” A funeral director has been jailed for 20 years for leaving dozens of bodies – including a miscarried baby – “rotting” in his mortuary and giving bereaved families the wrong ashes. Robert Bush, the owner of Legacy Independent Funeral Services in Hull, pleaded guilty to 67 offences spanning 12 years and affecting hundreds of families, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial. title: India’s monsoon rains in danger as UN chief warns planet is ‘on fire’
summary: António Guterres says strengthening El Niño will help push the world’s climate crisis into ‘uncharted territory’
body: India’s monsoon is in danger and hotter, drier conditions are forecast across much of the world as a stronger El Niño weather system is taking hold, weather experts have warned. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said the strengthening El Niño was “adding fuel to a planet already on fire” and pushing the world into “uncharted territory”. The El Niño system will strengthen from August to October, which will bring higher temperatures globally, with increasing rainfall in some regions while others suffer drought, according to data and forecasts released by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Friday. Marine heatwaves have already shocked scientists this year and are set to intensify: the WMO said temperatures were likely to exceed 2.9C above normal in several regions. “The Pacific waters driving it have never been this warm this early in an El Niño, and temperatures are still increasing,” Guterres said. “[This year] risks shattering every seasonal record, and driving even more severe effects worldwide. We are in uncharted territory.” The risk of a weakened monsoon, which brings the rain on which Indian farmers rely, was highlighted as the forecast gave an “enhancement in the probability for below-normal rainfall”, which would produce increased drought, floods and wildfire risk around the Indian Ocean basin. Drier conditions are also likely across parts of equatorial Africa to the west of the Horn of Africa, across the south and east of Australia, large parts of South America and in North America. Higher than normal rainfall is expected in southern Europe, central Asia and the Horn of Africa and south-eastern South America. Extreme weather has already caused havoc around the world this summer, with record-breaking heatwaves beginning in May in the UK, and wildfires across France and Spain that have destroyed villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people. Scientists have warned this year of the development of an El Niño, a weather system in the Pacific that frequently affects temperatures and rainfall around the world. Some El Niño years in the past have been relatively mild, but scientists have said that this year’s has been supercharged by the climate crisis. Warmer waters – earlier in the year than usual and with water temperatures still increasing – have led to predictions of a “super El Niño” forming. The WMO does not use this term, but has said that the weather system developing is likely to be significantly stronger and more intense than usual. Friday’s forecasts were the organisation’s latest update, covering August to October. Celeste Saulo, the secretary general of the WMO, called on governments to make preparations to help people affected by the heat, drought and potential floods that are likely in the months ahead. “El Niño is one of the most closely monitored climate phenomena in the world,” she said. “But forecasts in themselves do not prevent hazards, people do. This El Niño, developing against the backdrop of unprecedented ocean heat and rising temperatures, provides governments and communities with a window of opportunity to anticipate risks and act before impacts unfold. The decisions we make today will shape the impacts we experience tomorrow.” Guterres warned of the impacts on Friday and called for governments to take action on fossil fuels. “Two months ago, I warned that El Niño was arriving on our doorstep. Now it is inside the house, and turning up the heat,” he told reporters in New York. He added: “El Niño is strengthening – adding fuel to a planet already on fire with scorching heat domes, apocalyptic wildfires and record hot seas. Fossil fuels are fanning the flames of this crisis. Expansion must stop.” Guterres warned particularly of the risks to workers: “Heat is claiming lives on a growing scale, day after day, in every region of the world. It is also putting an enormous share of the global workforce at risk, exposing billions of people to dangers and often life-threatening conditions.” Separately, studies have shown that the extreme weather Europe is experiencing and the increasing likelihood of drought and wildfires have been “supercharged” by the climate crisis.

title: Ponds need more than a drop of protection
summary: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial arguing that freshwater havens require a law of their own
body: I agree with the need for protection of the vital habitat wildlife ponds create (Editorial, 24 July). One challenge to framing adequate legislation may be that some natural ponds tend to come and go. Many will dry out and gradually convert to boggy ground as plants take over, and new ponds will form. The Latin name for the common frog is Rana temporaria (temporary frog), reflecting that some of the pools in which frogs breed are not permanent. Thus we are trying to shield a moving target, which is more complicated than a wood, a river or a meadow that generally stay put. Of course, some ponds, like the Norfolk pingo ponds, are truly ancient and therefore easier to define and hence protect. The transitory nature of natural ponds may require a belt-and-braces approach that combines protection for places and for individual species. I would also emphasise the point you mention that ponds are a habitat which householders are able to create in their own gardens to magnificent effect. Our own ponds have breeding populations of frogs, toads and smooth and great crested newts. We regularly see grass snakes and water shrews, along with a huge variety of insect life (I have counted five species of dragonfly so far this summer). Garden ponds are not a substitute for fully wild natural habitats, but they are a vital component in supporting species affected by loss of habitat. Tim Franks Whaddon, Buckinghamshire • Re your editorial, perhaps at least part of the solution is for the government to work with farmers, landowners and water companies to find a way to reinstate ponds. It could also make environmental conservation plans go hand in hand with building and planning for mutually beneficial cooperation and thus safeguard conservation by creating natural habitats and integrating them with housing and development planning. The current plans appear to be shortsighted. Andy Burnham’s new government has a chance to show it is serious about delivering nature recovery – and not just the kind that fits neatly into its development plans. As for existing ponds, while the clean water bill is expected to be a step change, more is needed, and so we must be pressing to highlight the huge issues of nature recovery. Glenn Fish Sheffield • Great article on ponds. They are so vital, and overlooked by many. The farm I manage in Suffolk has 52, of which I have de-silted and renovated about 40. The need to hold water cannot be overestimated for nature, or even flood resilience. Glenn Buckingham Framsden, Suffolk • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: BP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for sale
summary: Move will end six decades of production in area, as new CEO tries to simplify company and cut debt
body: BP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale as it looks to end six decades of production from the basin. The firm announced on Friday morning it had launched a formal process to market its North Sea business for a potential sale. The move comes as BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, tries to simplify the company and cut its debt levels. O’Neill said: “The North Sea remains integral to the UK’s energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company.” She said Britain would “continue to play an important role” in BP’s future, adding: “We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day.” BP’s involvement in the North Sea dates back to 1964, when it was granted its first UK North Sea exploration licence. The company discovered the West Sole gasfield in the winter of 1965, followed by its largest discovery in the area, the giant Forties field, in 1970. BP’s planned exit from the North Sea comes as the climate crisis leads to wildfires and drought conditions across Europe. Angharad Hopkinson, a political campaigner at Greenpeace UK, called BP’s withdrawal from the North Sea “the canary in the coalmine for a toxic, declining basin”. She said: “If the North Sea really were the saviour of jobs, opportunity and energy security that the fossil fuel lobby claims, its biggest beneficiaries wouldn’t be heading for the exit.” On Thursday, Andy Burnham said he would take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, adding that the government could not ignore the potential energy resources it held. Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, described BP’s North Sea sale as “a watershed moment”. “It says a lot when BP isn’t prepared to stick around to see if the new government can re-energise the UK’s energy policy,” Beauchamp said. “Clearly BP thinks it will take too long at a time when the need to exploit new energy fields is pressing, and waiting around for Whitehall to move is not a prudent use of resources.” The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said she was in close contact with BP over its plans. “The North Sea is a vital national asset and we will take a pragmatic approach, recognising that oil and gas will be part of our energy mix for years to come,” she said. “I’m in close contact with BP and have made clear that my priority is ensuring that the workers and local community are protected during this sale process.” Since drilling began in the North Sea in the 1960s, 47.7bn barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) have been produced from the UK continental shelf as of the end of 2024. The North Sea Transition Authority estimated there to be 2.9bn BOE of UK oil and gas reserves left in the North Sea at the end of 2024. There is also an estimated 6.2bn BOE of contingent resources – petroleum estimated to be recoverable from known deposits but not ready for commercial development. There is an estimated 4.6bn BOE of “prospective resources” as well. These are undiscovered, potentially recoverable resources in mapped leads and prospects that have not yet been drilled. Those reserves could be extracted with government approval, if energy companies believed it was commercially viable. BP has been cutting its exposure to the UK this year. In May, it announced plans to sell stakes in two large carbon capture and storage projects in the north-east of England. The company said it would retain its UK aviation fuel distribution business, retail sites, UK-based trading desk and London headquarters. O’Neill took over as BP’s chief executive on 1 April. Less than two months later, the company removed its chair, Albert Manifold, citing serious concerns about “important governance standards, oversight and conduct”, which he denies.
